name: Berti Vogts
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1972 UEFA European Championship with West Germany and was named German Footballer of the Year in 1971 after winning back-to-back Bundesliga titles with Borussia Mönchengladbach.
early_history_summary: Vogts joined local club VfR Büttgen at age seven in 1954 and stayed until his 1965 transfer to Borussia Mönchengladbach, where he became a first-team regular in the Bundesliga at age 18. He earned his first senior cap for West Germany in 1967 at age 20 and was a key defender in Borussia's rise to Bundesliga dominance in the late 1960s and early 1970s, winning consecutive league titles in 1970 and 1971.
primary_early_advantage_tags: club youth system, Bundesliga ecosystem, national team pipeline
evidence_summary: Vogts spent eleven years in the VfR Büttgen youth system before joining Borussia Mönchengladbach at 18, immediately becoming a Bundesliga regular. He benefited from the German football pipeline of the 1960s, joining a club on the cusp of a golden era alongside players like Netzer, Heynckes, and Bonhof. By 25, he had won two Bundesliga titles, been named German Footballer of the Year, and won Euro 1972. No family background information was found in reviewed sources.

name: Karel Gott
milestone_by_age_26: Released his first solo single 'Moon River' in 1963, had the year's best-selling record in Czechoslovakia with 'Oči sněhem zaváté', and won his first Zlatý slavík (Golden Nightingale) award as the country's most popular singer.
early_history_summary: Gott trained as an electrician after failing art school exams, but was drawn to the Prague jazz scene. He began performing as an amateur in the late 1950s, failed a 1958 talent contest, but secured cafe performance slots. In 1960 he enrolled at the Prague Conservatory to study voice, released his first single with Supraphon in 1962, and broke through in 1963 with a place at the Semafor Theater and his first solo hit.
family_context_summary: Gott was born in Plzeň and moved to Prague at age six. His parents wanted him to become a worker and he initially trained as an electrician. No evidence of family financial advantage or musical background was found.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Parents preferred he pursue a trade rather than music.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Prague Conservatory, Semafor Theater, Konstantin Karenin mentorship
evidence_summary: Gott's path from electrician to national star was driven by his vocal talent, conservatory training under Konstantin Karenin (a student of Chaliapin), and the emerging Czechoslovak pop music scene centered on the Semafor Theater. He failed an early talent contest but persevered, releasing his first single at 23 and breaking through at 24 with a hit record and the Zlatý slavík award. His parents did not support a music career, and no family financial advantage was documented.

name: Thomas Bernhard
milestone_by_age_26: Published his first book, the poetry collection 'Auf der Erde und in der Hölle' (On Earth and in Hell) in 1957, following earlier poetry publications in literary journals starting in 1952.
early_history_summary: Bernhard was raised by his maternal grandparents in Austria, where his grandfather, the novelist Johannes Freumbichler, introduced him to literature and philosophy. He contracted tuberculosis as a youth and spent 1949-1951 in a sanatorium, where he began writing poetry. He worked as a court reporter and cultural journalist from 1951 to 1955, publishing poems and stories in newspapers. With financial support from the wealthy heiress Hedwig Stavianicek, he studied music at the Mozarteum from 1955 to 1957 and published his first poetry volume in 1957.
family_context_summary: Bernhard was born to an unwed Austrian mother who worked as a maid; his biological father refused to acknowledge him. He was raised largely by his maternal grandparents in Austria. His grandfather, the novelist Johannes Freumbichler, was a major literary influence.
parent_family_domain_summary: His grandfather Johannes Freumbichler was a novelist who introduced Bernhard to literature and philosophy, providing early intellectual mentorship. His mother worked as a maid and the family was not affluent.
primary_early_advantage_tags: grandfather novelist, Hedwig Stavianicek patronage, sanatorium writing, Mozarteum training
evidence_summary: Bernhard's early literary development was shaped by his grandfather Johannes Freumbichler's intellectual mentorship and the financial patronage of Hedwig Stavianicek, a wealthy heiress he met in a sanatorium at age 19. His tuberculosis diagnosis and sanatorium stay created both adversity and the conditions for sustained writing. He published poetry in journals from age 21 and his first book at 26, but his breakthrough novel 'Frost' did not arrive until age 32. The family was not affluent, but the grandfather's literary connections and Stavianicek's financial support were material advantages.

name: Didi
milestone_by_age_26: Played for Brazil in the 1954 FIFA World Cup, having already won the 1951 Carioca Championship and 1952 Copa Rio with Fluminense, and scored the first-ever goal at the Maracanã Stadium in 1950.
early_history_summary: Born into poverty in Campos dos Goytacazes, Didi sold peanuts as a child and nearly had his leg amputated at 14 due to infection. He began playing for local clubs in his hometown, turned professional with Madureira in 1947 at age 18, and joined Fluminense in 1949 at age 20, where he became a star over seven seasons. He made his Brazil national team debut in 1952 at age 23 and played in the 1954 World Cup at 25.
family_context_summary: Didi was born into a poor family in Campos dos Goytacazes, 150 miles north of Rio de Janeiro. He sold peanuts to help his family and began playing football in the streets. He nearly had his right leg amputated at age 14 due to a severe infection.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. Family was poor with no documented connection to professional football.
primary_early_advantage_tags: street football, poverty, near-amputation adversity, Rio football ecosystem
evidence_summary: Didi rose from extreme poverty in a small Brazilian city to become a Fluminense star and Brazil international by his mid-twenties. He began playing in the streets, turned professional at 18, and joined a major Rio club at 20. His early career was marked by adversity including near-amputation of his leg at 14. By 26, he had won state championships, scored the first goal at the Maracanã, and played in a World Cup. No family advantages were documented; his trajectory was driven by physical talent and persistence in the Rio football ecosystem.

name: Milan Kundera
milestone_by_age_26: Published his first book, the poetry collection 'Člověk zahrada širá' (Man: A Wide Garden) in 1953, and was appointed lecturer in world literature at the Film Faculty of the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague in 1952.
early_history_summary: Kundera was born into a middle-class family in Brno; his father was an important Czech musicologist and pianist who headed the Janáček Music Academy. He studied music and composition from his father before shifting to film studies at FAMU. He joined the Communist Party in 1947, was expelled in 1950, and was appointed a lecturer at FAMU in 1952. His first poetry collection was published in 1953, with subsequent volumes in 1955 and 1957.
family_context_summary: Kundera was born to a middle-class family in Brno. His father, Ludvík Kundera, was an important Czech musicologist and pianist who served as head of the Janáček Music Academy in Brno from 1948 to 1961. His mother was an educator.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father was a prominent musicologist and pianist who headed a major music academy, providing direct intellectual and cultural mentorship. Kundera learned piano and musicology from his father, and his cousin Ludvík Kundera was also a Czech writer and poet.
primary_early_advantage_tags: musicologist father, Janáček Academy, FAMU lecturer, Communist Party access
evidence_summary: Kundera benefited from a strong cultural and intellectual family platform: his father was a prominent musicologist who headed the Janáček Music Academy, providing early musical education and cultural capital. Kundera's cousin was also a writer. He leveraged this background into an academic position at FAMU by age 23 and published his first book at 24. His early works were propaganda-adjacent poetry that benefited from his Communist Party connections. His true literary fame came much later with 'The Joke' (1967) at age 38, but the first book publication at 24 is a material milestone.

name: Sid Vicious
milestone_by_age_26: Was the bassist for the Sex Pistols during the release of 'Never Mind the Bollocks, Here's the Sex Pistols' (October 1977), one of the most influential punk rock albums ever recorded.
early_history_summary: Born Simon John Ritchie in Lewisham, London, to a single mother who sold marijuana, Vicious grew up in turbulent circumstances across Kent and Hackney. He met John Lydon at technical college in 1973 and became part of the 'Four Johns' squatting circle. He was a regular at Malcolm McLaren and Vivienne Westwood's SEX clothing shop, the hub of the emerging London punk scene. He joined the Sex Pistols as bassist in early 1977 at age 19, replacing Glen Matlock, and appeared on their landmark debut album released in October 1977.
family_context_summary: Vicious was raised by a single mother, Anne Beverley, who dropped out of school and sold marijuana to get by. His father abandoned the family shortly after his birth. His stepfather died when he was young. The family lived in working-class conditions across Kent and East London.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father was a semi-professional trombone player on the London jazz scene, but abandoned the family. No evidence of musical training or industry connections transferred from parents.
primary_early_advantage_tags: London punk scene, SEX shop hub, Malcolm McLaren, John Lydon friendship, poverty
evidence_summary: Vicious's fame was driven by proximity to the London punk scene centered on McLaren and Westwood's SEX shop, his friendship with John Lydon, and the explosive cultural wave of punk rock in 1977. He had no musical training and was famously unable to play bass competently, yet his persona and the Sex Pistols' cultural moment made him an icon. His turbulent, impoverished upbringing with a drug-dealing mother created the conditions for his punk identity. He died at 21, so all achievements were before 26. The milestone is material despite his limited musical contribution, as the album is independently verifiable and culturally landmark.

name: Venkatraman Ramakrishnan
milestone_by_age_26: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 found. By 26, Ramakrishnan had completed a Ph.D. in physics (1976) and was beginning a postdoctoral transition to biology at UC San Diego. His Nobel Prize-winning ribosome work came decades later.
early_history_summary: Ramakrishnan was born in Chidambaram, India, to scientist parents—his father was a biochemist and his mother a biochemistry lecturer. He earned a B.Sc. in physics from Baroda University in 1971 at age 19, and a Ph.D. in physics from Ohio University in 1976 at age 24. He then switched to biology as a graduate student at UC San Diego before moving to a postdoc at Yale in 1978. His Nobel Prize in Chemistry came in 2009.
family_context_summary: Both parents were scientists: his father C.V. Ramakrishnan was a biochemist who did postdoctoral work with David Green at Madison, and his mother R. Rajalakshmi taught biochemistry at Annamalai University.
parent_family_domain_summary: Both parents were biochemists/scientists, providing a strong scientific household environment and intellectual mentorship from an early age.
evidence_summary: Ramakrishnan had strong scientific family background (both parents were biochemists) and completed his Ph.D. by 24, but no material career milestone occurred by age 26. His transition to biology began around 1976-78, and his Nobel Prize-winning ribosome structural work came in the 2000s. A Ph.D. completion is an academic credential, not a material independently verifiable public milestone in the sense required by the rubric.

name: Gordon Banks
milestone_by_age_26: Played in two FA Cup finals with Leicester City (1961 and 1963) and was an established First Division goalkeeper by his mid-twenties, having been transferred from Chesterfield to Leicester City in 1959.
early_history_summary: Banks was born in Sheffield to a working-class family; his father was a steelworker who ran an illegal betting shop. He left school at 15, worked as a coal bagger and bricklayer, and joined Chesterfield's youth team in 1953 at age 15. He played in the 1956 FA Youth Cup final, made his first-team debut in November 1958 at 20, and was sold to Leicester City in July 1959. He played in the 1961 and 1963 FA Cup finals with Leicester before winning the League Cup in 1964 and the World Cup in 1966.
family_context_summary: Banks was born in Abbeydale, Sheffield, to a working-class family. His father was a steelworker who later set up an illegal betting shop. Banks left school at 15 to work as a coal bagger and bricklayer. His disabled brother was mugged and died of his injuries.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of football connections in the family.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Sheffield schoolboys, Chesterfield youth, working-class background, physical labor
evidence_summary: Banks rose from a working-class Sheffield background to become a professional goalkeeper through the English football pipeline. He joined Chesterfield at 15, played in the FA Youth Cup final at 18, and broke into the first team at 20. His transfer to Leicester City at 21 gave him a First Division platform, and he reached two FA Cup finals by 25. His early jobs as a coal bagger and bricklayer built physical strength. No family football connections or financial advantages were documented; his trajectory was driven by physical talent and the club youth system.

name: Rudolf Schenker
milestone_by_age_26: Released the Scorpions' debut album 'Lonesome Crow' in 1972, having founded the band in 1965 at age 16 and built it into a performing act over seven years.
early_history_summary: Schenker was born in Hildesheim, Germany, and initially wanted to be a professional soccer player. He received his first guitar at 16 after asking his father for a motorbike and being refused. He taught himself chords from a book ordered from Holland, formed the Scorpions in 1965 at age 16, and played local clubs in the Hanover area. He met vocalist Klaus Meine around 1968, forming a durable songwriting partnership. The band's debut album 'Lonesome Crow' was released in 1972 on Metronome Records, with Schenker's younger brother Michael also in the lineup.
family_context_summary: Schenker was born in Hildesheim, Germany. His father bought him his first guitar (a Framus) when he was 16. His younger brother Michael Schenker also became a renowned guitarist and was an early member of the Scorpions before joining UFO.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father supported his musical interest by purchasing his first guitar. His younger brother Michael was a guitar prodigy who joined the Scorpions, creating a sibling collaboration in the band's early years.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught guitar, band founding, Klaus Meine partnership, brother Michael Schenker
evidence_summary: Schenker's path was driven by self-directed persistence: he taught himself guitar from a book, formed the Scorpions at 16, and spent seven years playing local clubs before securing a record deal. His father bought his first guitar but was not a musician. His brother Michael was a guitar prodigy who contributed to the debut album. The songwriting partnership with Klaus Meine, formed around 1968, was a durable complementary team. The debut album at 23 is a material milestone, though the band's major international success came years later in the 1980s.

name: Ei-ichi Negishi
milestone_by_age_26: No material, independently verifiable milestone by age 26 found. By 26, Negishi had graduated from the University of Tokyo (1958) and was a Ph.D. student at the University of Pennsylvania on a Fulbright scholarship. His Nobel Prize-winning palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling work was developed in the mid-1970s when he was in his late thirties and early forties.
early_history_summary: Negishi was born in 1935 in Changchun, China (then Manchukuo), as a Japanese citizen, and grew up in Korea and Japan after WWII. He graduated from the University of Tokyo in 1958 with a degree in applied chemistry, worked as a research chemist at Teijin Limited, and received a Fulbright scholarship to pursue a Ph.D. at the University of Pennsylvania in 1960. He completed his Ph.D. in 1963 under Allan R. Day, then became a postdoctoral researcher with Nobel laureate Herbert C. Brown at Purdue in 1966.
family_context_summary: Negishi was born to a Japanese family in Manchuria; the family moved to Korea and then back to Japan after WWII, settling in an underdeveloped area near Tokyo where his father attempted farming. The family of seven faced food shortages in the postwar years.
parent_family_domain_summary: Not documented in reviewed sources. No evidence of scientific or academic family background.
evidence_summary: Negishi's early career was a conventional academic path: University of Tokyo degree, industrial research position, Fulbright scholarship, and Ph.D. at Penn. By 26, he was a Ph.D. student with no independently verifiable material milestone. His Nobel Prize-winning work on palladium-catalyzed cross-coupling was developed in the mid-1970s when he was approximately 40. Postwar adversity shaped his early years but did not produce a milestone by 26.

name: Pierre Boulez
milestone_by_age_26: Was appointed stage music director of the Compagnie Renaud-Barrault in 1946 and had composed significant early works including 'Sonatine pour flûte et piano' and the 'Première Sonate for piano', establishing himself as a leading young avant-garde composer by the early 1950s.
early_history_summary: Boulez was born in Montbrison, France, the son of an engineer. He studied advanced mathematics in Lyon before defying his father's wishes to pursue music. He was admitted to the Paris Conservatoire in 1944, studied composition with Olivier Messiaen, and learned twelve-tone technique with René Leibowitz. He graduated with highest honors in 1945. In 1946, at age 21, he was appointed stage music director of the Compagnie Renaud-Barrault, a major professional position. His early compositions including the Sonatine and Première Sonate established his reputation as a leading avant-garde composer.
family_context_summary: Boulez was the son of Léon Boulez, an engineer (described as a steel manufacturer by Britannica). The family was middle-class; his father wanted him to pursue engineering, but Boulez defied this to study music. He had a stillborn older sibling and a sister born in 1922.
parent_family_domain_summary: His father was an engineer, providing a mathematically rigorous household environment. Boulez studied advanced mathematics before switching to music, which informed his compositional approach. No direct musical family background was documented.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Paris Conservatoire, Messiaen mentorship, Leibowitz twelve-tone training, Renaud-Barrault position
evidence_summary: Boulez benefited from elite institutional training at the Paris Conservatoire under Olivier Messiaen and private twelve-tone instruction from René Leibowitz, both major figures in 20th-century music. His mathematical background from his engineer father's influence shaped his compositional approach. By 21, he held a professional position at the Compagnie Renaud-Barrault and had composed works that established his avant-garde reputation. The concentration of high-level mentors and the Paris post-war musical ecosystem were catalytic. His father opposed the music career, so family financial support was limited.

name: Hiroaki Sato
milestone_by_age_26: Debuted for the Japan national team on January 2, 1955, and won the 1955 Emperor's Cup with Kwangaku Club, later representing Japan at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics.
early_history_summary: Sato was born in Amagasaki, Hyogo, Japan. He attended Amagasaki High School and then Kwansei Gakuin University from 1951 to 1954. After graduating, he joined Kwangaku Club, a team composed of his university's players and graduates. He debuted for the Japan national team on January 2, 1955, at age 22, and won the Emperor's Cup in 1955, 1958, and 1959. He played at the 1956 Melbourne Olympics and the 1958 Asian Games, earning 15 caps for Japan.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Kwansei Gakuin University, Kwangaku Club, Japan national team
evidence_summary: Sato's path to national team selection ran through the Japanese university football system: he played at Kwansei Gakuin University and then for the associated Kwangaku Club. He debuted for Japan at 22 and won the Emperor's Cup the same year. He represented Japan at the 1956 Olympics at 24. No family background or financial information was documented in reviewed sources. His achievements are notable within Japanese football but he is primarily known to specialists, consistent with a tier-4 designation.
